chunks.text: A graduate resume for Singapore employers runs to one page unless you have over five years of experience. Recruiters spend under a minute on the first pass, so the top third of the page must carry the strongest evidence: current degree, graduation date, and your two or three most job-relevant skills.

Standard section order for an early-career applicant: contact block, education, work and internship experience, projects, skills, then optional extras such as volunteering or certifications. Put education first while you are still studying; move experience above education once you have more than one full-time role.

The contact block needs a professional email address, a mobile number you actually answer, and optionally a LinkedIn or portfolio URL. It does not need your full mailing address, your date of birth, or a photograph. Those fields are not used by most Singapore employers and take up space you need for evidence.

Write the education entry as institution, degree or programme, major, expected graduation month and year, and any honours or GPA if it helps you. If grades are added, state the scale: a 4.2 without saying it is out of 5.0 tells the reader nothing. List relevant coursework only when it maps directly to the role.

Never state a skill you cannot demonstrate in an interview. Graduate recruiters routinely probe the first two items on a skills list. An inflated skills section converts a strong application into a credibility problem, and in Singapore a false claim on an application can also be a contractual issue.

Coursework projects count as experience when they show scope and ownership. Name the project, state what you personally built, the tools you used, and one result. "Built the retrieval layer for a four-person capstone, cutting query latency by 40 percent" is evidence; "worked on an AI project" is a label.

Use STAR for each bullet: Situation, Task, Action, Result. In a resume you compress it to one line - strong verb, what you did, with what, and the outcome. The interviewer reads the result first; if there is no result the bullet reads as a job description rather than an accomplishment.

Lead every bullet with a concrete verb: built, automated, migrated, reduced, designed, measured, shipped, debugged. Avoid "responsible for", "helped with", "involved in", and "assisted", which describe proximity to work rather than contribution. A hiring manager cannot score proximity.

Quantify when you honestly can: percent faster, items processed, users served, hours saved, error rate reduced, budget managed. If you have no measurement, quantify scope instead - team size, dataset size, number of releases, duration. A real count beats an invented percentage.

Keep bullets to one or two lines each. A bullet that wraps to four lines stops being scannable and usually contains two separate claims. Split it, or cut the weaker half. Three to five strong bullets per role is the working range; more than that and none of them get read properly.

Most large employers parse resumes with an applicant tracking system before a human sees them. Plain single-column layouts, standard section headings, and no text inside images or tables are the practical rules. Fancy two-column templates frequently reorder your content into nonsense during parsing.

Mirror the vocabulary the job description actually uses. If the posting says "natural language processing" and your resume says "text analytics", the keyword match may fail even though the work is equivalent. Use both phrasings once, in the skills section and in a bullet, rather than repeating one.

Spell out acronyms once with the expansion in brackets: RAG (retrieval augmented generation), ETL (extract, transform, load), NLP (natural language processing). Different systems index differently, and some search the expansion while others search the acronym.

Group skills into two or three labelled lines - languages, frameworks and tools, then domain skills - rather than one long undifferentiated list. Keep a skill in the list only if it appears somewhere else in the resume as evidence. A skills line with no supporting bullet is a claim the reader cannot check.

Tailoring a resume is three passes, not a rewrite. First map the posting's stated requirements to your own evidence and mark what is missing. Second reorder and reword so the matched items appear in the top third and use the posting's vocabulary. Third cut anything irrelevant to this role. Budget fifteen to twenty minutes per application once practised.

Do not rewrite the resume for every posting from scratch. Keep one master document holding every bullet you might use, then produce a tailored one-pager per application by selecting and reordering. The master is where you add new work; the tailored copy is disposable.

When a requirement is genuinely missing, do not manufacture it. Either leave it out, or - if you have adjacent evidence - state the adjacent thing precisely and let the reader judge the transfer. "One term of applied statistics coursework using R" is honest and sometimes sufficient. "Proficient in R" when you have not used it since is not.

Keep the summary line specific to the target role and three lines at most. It should name the role family, your strongest two or three relevant capabilities, and what you are looking for. Generic objectives copied across applications actively weaken a graduate resume because they signal a bulk send.

Before submitting, check four things: the file is a PDF named with your own name, the contact details are current, every date is internally consistent, and the same role title does not appear twice. Then read it aloud once. Sentences that are hard to say aloud are usually also hard to read.

AI/ML role checklist, core: Python or a comparable language; applied machine learning; supervised and unsupervised learning; model evaluation including cross-validation and held-out sets; feature engineering; and the ability to read and critique a model's error analysis rather than only its headline accuracy.

AI/ML frameworks commonly named in postings: PyTorch, TensorFlow with Keras, and scikit-learn for classical models. Also expected: pandas and NumPy for data manipulation, and a plotting library for diagnostics. Being able to say which framework you used for what, and why, matters more than listing all three.

NLP stack for graduate roles: text preprocessing and tokenisation, classical text classification, and an awareness of transformer-based models. Familiarity with Hugging Face tooling and the ability to evaluate a text model with precision, recall and F1 rather than accuracy alone is a common screening point.

For LLM-adjacent roles, the expected baseline includes prompting technique, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over a private document set, and vector database concepts such as embedding similarity search. Interviewers usually ask what you did when retrieval returned irrelevant passages, so prepare that failure case.

MLOps expectations for an early-career hire are modest but specific: packaging a trained model behind an API, basic containerisation with Docker, version control with Git for notebooks as well as code, and enough logging to tell why a prediction was made. Model deployment experience outranks hyperparameter tuning.

AI/ML roles assume competent SQL: joins, aggregations, window functions, and the ability to sanity-check a table before modelling on it. A candidate who can describe a data quality problem they found and how they handled it reads as more senior than one who only lists modelling techniques.

Typical graduate AI/ML responsibilities: cleaning and preparing datasets, training and evaluating baseline models, writing reproducible experiment code, documenting results, and communicating limitations to non-technical stakeholders. The last item is the one that separates candidates, because it is where trust is built.

Adjacent evidence that legitimately counts toward AI/ML requirements: statistics coursework for model evaluation, data engineering work for pipeline skills, and any project where you deployed something other people used. State the specific activity, not the label. "Built the evaluation harness for a four-person project" maps to model evaluation.

Software engineering core checklist: proficiency in at least one general-purpose language at a level where you can debug unfamiliar code; solid Git workflow including branching and resolving conflicts; the ability to write unit tests; and comfort reading someone else's codebase before writing your own.

Backend expectations: designing and consuming REST APIs, understanding HTTP status codes and auth headers, input validation, and knowing what happens at a network boundary. A candidate who can explain how they handled a failing third-party API in production is answering the reliability question interviewers actually care about.

Testing expectations for graduates: unit tests for pure logic, integration tests across a boundary, and the habit of reproducing a bug as a failing test before fixing it. Naming a framework (pytest, JUnit) matters less than being able to describe a test that caught a real regression.

Delivery tooling: Docker for reproducible environments, CI/CD pipelines that run tests on every push, and eventually Kubernetes or a managed equivalent. For a graduate role, having configured a CI workflow that ran tests and blocked a bad merge is strong, concrete evidence.

Architecture vocabulary that postings use and interviews probe: microservices versus a modular monolith, synchronous versus event-driven communication, caching layers, and idempotency. You are not expected to have designed these at scale, but you are expected to reason about trade-offs without hand-waving.

Most software roles touch a database. Expected: schema basics, indexing intuition, and SQL that goes beyond SELECT star. Being able to explain why a query was slow, and what you changed, is a common practical interview question for backend-leaning graduate roles.

Process expectations: working in short increments, writing a clear pull request description, reviewing others' code without ego, and estimating honestly. Agile and Scrum appear in nearly every posting; mentioning a specific ceremony you contributed to is more credible than listing the framework name.

Adjacent evidence that counts toward software engineering requirements: scripts written to automate your own work, a personal project with users, coursework in algorithms and data structures, and any contribution to an open-source repository. State what the code did and how it was verified.

Data analytics core checklist: advanced SQL including joins, window functions and CTEs; Python or R for analysis; spreadsheet competence beyond basic formulas; and the statistical literacy to know when a difference is meaningful. The most common screening task is a take-home analysis, so the ability to explain your method matters.

Statistics for analysts: distributions and when they mislead, sampling and selection bias, confidence intervals, significance testing, and the difference between correlation and a causal claim. Expect an interview question about a metric that moved and whether the change was real or noise.

Experimentation: designing an A/B test including the hypothesis, the unit of randomisation, the primary metric, and the sample you need before you start. The failure mode interviewers probe is stopping a test early because the result looked good, and then reporting the peak as the finding.

Visualisation and reporting: choose the chart before the tool. Time series get lines, comparisons get bars, distributions get histograms or box plots, relationships get scatter plots. Avoid pie charts with more than four slices. Tableau and Power BI both appear in postings; naming one with a concrete dashboard is enough.

Analyst data plumbing: pulling from a warehouse rather than a CSV export, writing a repeatable query instead of one-off edits, and documenting definitions so two people compute the same metric the same way. ETL concepts and tools such as Airflow or dbt are increasingly listed even for analyst roles.

Tooling vocabulary that helps in analytics postings: pandas for manipulation, NumPy for numerics, matplotlib or seaborn for diagnostics, and a warehouse such as BigQuery or Snowflake. Excel remains required in most business-facing analyst roles, particularly pivot tables and lookups.

The analyst's core deliverable is a decision, not a chart. Write the headline first, then the evidence. Interviews routinely ask you to explain a technical finding to a non-technical stakeholder in two sentences, so practise compressing without losing the caveat.

Adjacent evidence that counts toward analytics requirements: coursework involving a dataset you had to clean yourself, a report where you chose the metric, and any role where you were the person others asked for a number. State the dataset size and the decision it informed.

Product management core checklist for graduates: articulating a user problem before proposing a solution, writing a clear problem statement and acceptance criteria, prioritising with a stated rationale, and communicating trade-offs to engineering and design. The bar is structured thinking, not seniority.

User research expectations: writing non-leading interview questions, running a small study without wasting participants' time, and synthesising findings into themes rather than anecdotes. Being able to say what would change your mind, and what evidence you would need, is the mark of a credible junior PM.

Product metrics vocabulary: activation, retention, engagement, and the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator. Choose one primary metric and at most two guardrail metrics. Applying for a role without being able to name the metric you would move is a common and avoidable mistake.

Prioritisation frameworks appear in postings and interviews: RICE, MoSCoW, impact versus effort. What is being tested is not the acronym but whether you can explain why you sequenced work that way, and what you deliberately chose not to do this quarter.

Delivery process expectations: writing user stories, maintaining a groomed backlog, running a stand-up without letting it become a status report, and defining what done means. Familiarity with Jira or a comparable tracker is assumed; a concrete example of a backlog decision you owned is better.

Stakeholder management: identifying who is affected, what each party optimises for, and how to surface a disagreement before it becomes a blocker. Graduate PMs are expected to escalate early and with a recommendation rather than a problem statement.

Market and competitive analysis: define the segment, name the alternatives the user has today including doing nothing, and state your differentiation in one sentence. Analysts are expected to read a product's public documentation and pricing page and infer its likely strategy.

Adjacent evidence that counts toward product management requirements: leading a student project end to end including scope decisions, running a survey or set of interviews, and any role where you wrote requirements someone else implemented. State what you decided and what happened as a result.
